context.audience: Marketing, media, and franchise marketing leaders at quick-service restaurant (QSR) chains, fast-casual brands, and casual dining chains. Franchise-model QSRs (McDonald's, Burger King, Subway) involve a complex two-tier media structure: national brand campaigns funded by system-wide advertising cooperative contributions (typically 4–5% of gross sales), plus local/regional franchise media funded separately by individual franchisees or multi-unit operators. Audiences range from mass-market everyday value seekers to loyalty program members who transact through apps. QSR also increasingly addresses delivery-occasion consumers through third-party platforms (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub).
pain_points: National cooperative vs. local franchisee media tension: national ad co-op campaigns are designed for brand building and LTO (limited time offer) promotion, but individual franchisees need market-specific media that drives traffic to their specific locations — these priorities regularly conflict, particularly in markets where the brand is strong nationally but a local franchisee faces unique competitive threats

Third-party delivery platform cannibalizing first-party digital ordering: DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Grubhub charge 15–30% commission on each order, yet brands have historically invested media in driving awareness that converts through these platforms rather than their own apps — 40% of QSR brands are now actively redirecting media investment toward first-party digital ordering

Daypart and occasion media allocation complexity: QSR has 5+ distinct dayparts (breakfast, lunch, afternoon snack, dinner, late night) each with different target audiences, competitive dynamics, and offer strategies — allocating national media budget across dayparts without over-investing in already-strong ones (e.g., breakfast dominance for some chains) is a chronic planning challenge

LTO (limited time offer) media compression: new LTO launches require intense 4–6 week media campaigns to drive trial and generate cultural buzz before the item is pulled — with 3–4 LTOs per year per brand, media teams are perpetually in launch mode with little budget remaining for evergreen brand or loyalty campaigns

Measuring media impact on same-store sales (SSS) in a multi-causal environment: SSS is influenced by weather, competitive activity, commodity prices, staffing levels, and local economic conditions — isolating the media contribution requires sophisticated matched-market testing that many QSR brands still don't run

Loyalty app and digital data maturity gap: while McDonald's has 46 million 90-day active US loyalty users and Starbucks is a digital-native brand, the majority of mid-tier QSR and fast-casual brands have immature app and CRM infrastructure, making first-party data activation and personalized media impossible
kpis: Same-store sales (SSS) growth in media-active markets vs. control markets — ultimate business outcome metric
Digital order mix percentage (owned app + website) vs. third-party delivery — measures direct channel shift success
App download and 90-day active user count — indicator of loyalty program health and first-party data asset growth
Cost per visit / cost per transaction (measured via location data partners like Placer.ai, Foursquare, or SafeGraph)
LTO trial rate in launch markets — what percentage of target customers tried the new menu item during its campaign window
Average unit volume (AUV) contribution attributed to media-driven traffic vs. organic repeat visits
Loyalty member spend per visit vs. non-loyalty customer average — validates loyalty media investment
context.regulatory: FTC truth-in-advertising requirements apply to food advertising, particularly health and nutritional claims. Menu labeling regulations (FDA requires calorie disclosure for chains with 20+ locations). Children's advertising restrictions for QSR — CARU guidelines limit advertising of food products to children under 12 that don't meet nutritional standards. Social media influencer disclosure (#ad) required for paid food creator partnerships. Alcohol advertising restrictions for brands serving beer/wine. ADA accessibility standards for digital ordering and app-based media. State-level restrictions on toy/prize bundling in children's meals (California).
context.seasonality: QSR is less seasonal than some categories but has clear promotional peaks. Summer (May–Aug) is highest traffic volume for most QSR — beverages, ice cream, and value platforms drive frequency. Back-to-school (Aug–Sep) creates family occasion and convenience-meal traffic. Q4 holiday season (Nov–Dec) is particularly strong for family dining occasions. New Year (Jan) drives 'better-for-you' menu and salad promotion windows. Super Bowl (early Feb) is largest single-day QSR sales occasion — creates intense media competition around game-day value messaging. Ramadan and other cultural calendar moments increasingly important for brands with diverse customer bases.
context.budget_dynamics: QSR is one of the highest-frequency advertising categories — major chains are in market 52 weeks per year. National cooperative budgets at top chains are massive: McDonald's US system ad fund alone generates $800M–$1B annually from franchisee contributions. Streaming and digital channels growing fastest — major QSR chains are leading the shift from linear TV to streaming/CTV to deliver locally specific messaging and creative versioning. 'We are increasing culturally relevant marketing in digital, social, and streaming channels' — Wendy's 2026 strategy. Social media has become the primary cultural conversation channel for QSR — viral TikTok moments, limited drops, and creator partnerships now part of every major launch. Digital sales growing: Domino's digital exceeded 80% of sales; QSR digital mix averaging 25–35%, targeting 50–60% by 2030.
channels_that_work: Streaming and Connected TV (CTV) — QSR brands are leaders in streaming adoption; iSpot research notes 'QSR brands are one of the best examples for how advertisers can effectively utilize streaming to reach their intended audience'; enables locally specific messaging and creative versioning by market or daypart

Linear TV — still core for national tent-pole campaigns (Super Bowl, NFL sponsorships) and mass-reach brand building; major QSR chains among TV's largest advertisers but shifting allocation toward streaming

Paid social (TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat) — QSR is culturally driven; 76% of consumers say online food content inspires purchases; TikTok food discovery drives impulse traffic; Snapchat users 2.7x more likely to engage with brand links
Creator and influencer marketing — food creators drive LTO awareness and viral moments at scale; partnerships with food-focused micro and macro creators are standard in LTO launch playbooks
Programmatic display and geofencing — radius targeting around restaurant locations to capture nearby consumers; competitive geofencing (targeting competitor locations) common tactic for conquest
Paid search (local and national) — 'near me' and specific food item queries; voice search growing for food and restaurant discovery
Streaming audio and podcasts — drive-time and food/cooking podcast adjacency; Spotify contextual targeting for 'food' and 'dining' playlist listeners
measurement_challenges: Attribution of media to in-restaurant visit: most QSR transactions are cash or card with no digital identity — connecting media exposure to purchase requires third-party location data (Placer.ai, Foursquare) or card-linked transaction matching (Visa, Mastercard data partnerships), both with coverage limitations

Same-store sales variance explained by media: SSS is simultaneously affected by weather, staffing, commodity prices, pricing changes, and competitive events — cleanly isolating media contribution requires matched-market or holdout designs that national co-op campaigns are structurally unable to run at scale

LTO trial measurement: knowing what percentage of media-exposed consumers actually tried the limited-time menu item requires either POS-linked first-party data (available only for app orders) or panel research that is expensive and slow

Delivery platform conversion leakage: a consumer sees a QSR ad on social, searches for the brand, and places an order through DoorDash — the media team served a paid impression that converted through a third-party platform with no first-party attribution

Daypart-level media attribution: a breakfast campaign impressions served at 6am don't convert until 9am when the consumer drives past the location — time-lag between media exposure and transaction is difficult to isolate in aggregate reporting
subtopics: National co-op media management for franchise QSR brands
LTO (limited time offer) launch media strategy: trial generation and urgency
First-party digital ordering migration: app download and retention media
Daypart-specific media planning: breakfast, lunch, dinner, and late-night occasions
QSR value platform advertising: communicating price leadership in inflationary environment
Delivery occasion media: third-party platform vs. owned digital ordering
Loyalty program activation media: CRM-connected, personalized frequency campaigns
Local and regional QSR franchisee media programs
context.typical_budget_range: Independent restaurant or small regional chain (10–50 locations): $100K–$1M/year. Regional fast-casual brand (50–200 locations): $3M–$15M/year. Mid-size QSR chain (200–1,000 locations): $20M–$75M/year. National QSR chain (McDonald's, Subway, Taco Bell tier): $500M–$1.5B+/year across national co-op + local. Note: franchise model means 4–5% of gross system sales flow into the national advertising cooperative, often totaling hundreds of millions annually.
context.buying_model: National co-op campaigns planned and bought by AOR (agency of record) typically held co at major agencies (DDB, FCB, TBWA, Leo Burnett). TV upfront bought by national AOR; digital and programmatic via integrated agency or specialized performance shop. Local franchisee media: smaller agency networks, DSPs, or franchise marketing platforms. Social bought self-serve or via agency social team with brand approval gates. Creator partnerships via talent agencies or influencer marketing platforms. Location data measurement via Placer.ai, SafeGraph, or Foursquare integrated into media reporting. Streaming audio and podcast bought direct or programmatically.
context.creative_considerations: Food photography and videography quality is non-negotiable — 'hero shots' of the product must make food look appetizing in any format. Social-native content (TikTok vertical video, Instagram Reels) performs best when it feels authentic and creator-generated, not polished brand advertising. Limited time offer urgency must be communicated clearly — countdown language and bold visual calls-out work in display and social formats. Humor and cultural relevance outperform rational benefit messaging for QSR brand campaigns (McDonald's 'CosMc's,' Wendy's social voice, Taco Bell cultural moments). Personalization opportunity: app-connected media can serve loyalty members with offers relevant to their order history — highest CTR creative in QSR. Breakfast and late-night creative requires entirely different tone and occasion context than lunch/dinner campaigns.
